name: pastry cream
instructions:
Classic french crème pâtissière — thick, egg-yolk-based vanilla custard cooked on the stovetop with cornstarch as the thickener. The base building-block for filled pastries (éclairs, cream puffs, tarts, mille-feuille) and a rich topping/filling for cakes. Ephemeral topping — best within 2-3 days of making; doesn't freeze well.

MAKES ~2 cups. Stovetop; ~15 min active + chill time.

=== INGREDIENTS ===

- 2 cups whole milk
- 1/2 cup granulated sugar (split: 1/4 cup with the milk, 1/4 cup with the yolks)
- pinch of salt
- 4-6 large egg yolks (4 for softer, 6 for richer/firmer)
- 3 tbsp cornstarch
- 2 tbsp unsalted butter, cubed
- 1 tsp vanilla extract (or 1/2 vanilla bean, split and scraped — add to milk in step 1 if using)

=== PROCEDURE ===

1. HEAT THE MILK: in a medium saucepan, combine the milk with 1/4 cup of the sugar and the pinch of salt (and vanilla bean scrapings/pod if using — pull the pod out later). Heat over medium until steaming and just about to simmer — small bubbles at the edges. Don't boil.

2. WHISK THE YOLK BASE: while the milk heats, in a separate bowl, whisk the egg yolks with the remaining 1/4 cup sugar and the cornstarch until pale, thick, and smooth. Cornstarch should be fully dissolved with no lumps.

3. TEMPER THE YOLKS: with the milk hot but not boiling, slowly pour about 1/3 of the hot milk into the yolk mixture WHILE WHISKING CONSTANTLY. This warms the yolks gradually so they don't scramble when they hit the full heat. Then pour the tempered yolk mixture back into the saucepan with the remaining milk.

4. COOK TO THICKEN: over medium heat, whisk constantly. The mixture will look thin at first, then rapidly thicken as the starch and yolks cook (~2-4 min). Continue whisking through the thickening.

5. HOLD AT A BOIL FOR 30-60 SECONDS: once it starts bubbling (proper bubbles breaking the surface, not just steaming), keep whisking and cook for at least 30 seconds — 60 is safer. This step is load-bearing (see notes) — it fully cooks the cornstarch and eliminates any raw-starch taste, and also inactivates an enzyme in the yolks that would otherwise break the custard down over time.

6. OFF HEAT, ADD BUTTER + VANILLA: remove from heat. Whisk in the butter cubes one at a time until fully incorporated and the pastry cream is glossy. Whisk in the vanilla extract (if not using a vanilla bean) at this stage.

7. STRAIN (OPTIONAL BUT RECOMMENDED): pour through a fine-mesh strainer into a clean bowl to catch any bits of cooked yolk or cornstarch lumps. Gives a perfectly smooth finish.

8. PLASTIC WRAP DIRECTLY ON THE SURFACE: cover the pastry cream with plastic wrap PRESSED DIRECTLY onto the surface (touching it, no air gap). This prevents a skin from forming as it cools. Refrigerate at least 2 hours until fully chilled.

9. WHISK BEFORE USING: after chilling, the pastry cream will be set stiff. Whisk vigorously by hand (or with an electric mixer briefly) to loosen it back to a smooth, spreadable consistency before using.
notes:
Classic french pastry cream (crème pâtissière). Foundational technique — worth learning because it opens the door to éclairs, cream puffs, fruit tarts, mille-feuille, and any number of filled pastries or cake toppings.

=== TEMPERING IS LOAD-BEARING — DON'T POUR ALL THE HOT MILK IN AT ONCE ===

Egg yolks scramble at ~150°F (65°C). Hot milk is well over that. If you pour all the hot milk into the raw yolks at once, or (worse) dump the yolks straight into the hot milk, you'll cook the yolks into scrambled egg bits suspended in the custard.

Tempering = pouring a small amount (~1/3) of hot milk into the yolks SLOWLY while whisking constantly. This warms the yolks up in a controlled way. Once the yolks are warm, adding them back to the rest of the hot milk is safe — the yolks are close enough to the milk temperature that they won't shock-cook.

=== HOLD AT A BOIL FOR 30-60 SECONDS — TWO REASONS ===

When the custard starts bubbling, keep whisking and let it boil for 30-60 seconds. Load-bearing for two independent reasons:

1. COOKS THE CORNSTARCH: raw or under-cooked cornstarch tastes chalky and raw. The boil ensures the starch gelatinizes fully and the flavor is clean.
2. INACTIVATES AN ENZYME IN THE YOLKS: egg yolks contain alpha-amylase, an enzyme that breaks down starch. If you don't cook the custard hot enough to inactivate the enzyme, the pastry cream will slowly break down and get runny in the fridge over several hours. Boiling for 30-60 seconds deactivates the enzyme and the custard stays thick.

Don't just pull it off heat the moment it thickens — hold it at a low boil for the extra minute.

=== PLASTIC WRAP DIRECTLY ON THE SURFACE ===

When pastry cream cools uncovered (or covered with an air gap), a rubbery skin forms on top. To prevent: press plastic wrap flat against the surface of the cream — touching it, no air between wrap and cream. Then refrigerate.

Skip this step and you'll have a skin to strain out (or work around) when you use the cream. Not the end of the world but easy to prevent.

=== WHISK BEFORE USING — SETS STIFF IN THE FRIDGE ===

Chilled pastry cream sets quite stiff. Whisk vigorously by hand (or with a mixer briefly) before using to loosen it back to a smooth, pipeable/spreadable consistency. Straight from the fridge without whisking, it's too stiff to spread cleanly.

=== USES — WHAT PASTRY CREAM IS FOR ===

- CAKE TOPPING / FILLING — pairs cleanly with lighter cakes ([[french-yogurt-cake]] is a natural fit; see that recipe's ephemeral-toppings framing) topped with fresh fruit
- FILLING FOR CREAM PUFFS, ÉCLAIRS, MILLE-FEUILLE — the classical uses
- BASE FOR FRUIT TARTS — spread in the tart shell, top with sliced fresh fruit
- BASE FOR OTHER CREAMS: fold in whipped cream → DIPLOMAT CREAM (lighter); whisk in soft butter → GERMAN BUTTERCREAM (thicker, cake-frosting-worthy)

=== EPHEMERAL — 2-3 DAYS MAX, DOESN'T FREEZE ===

Pastry cream is best within 2-3 days of making. It gets watery / weepy over time as the custard breaks down (even if you cooked it properly), and the dairy-and-yolk base doesn't age gracefully past a few days.

Does NOT freeze well — the emulsion breaks on thaw. Make what you'll use.

=== YOLK COUNT — 4 FOR SOFTER, 6 FOR RICHER ===

4 yolks gives you a softer, more spreadable pastry cream. 6 yolks gives you a richer, firmer result that holds shape better (good for piping). Standard french recipes usually land at 5-6; american recipes lean lighter at 4. Both work; pick based on what you're using it for.

=== WHOLE MILK, NOT REDUCED FAT ===

Whole milk is the standard. Reduced-fat or skim milk makes a thinner, less-rich pastry cream — technically works but noticeably less satisfying. Half-and-half or cream would push it into a richer direction (more like a crème anglaise base) — fine to experiment with but not the classical build.

=== SIBLING / RELATED ===

- [[french-yogurt-cake]]: natural cake pairing — see that recipe's ephemeral-topping framing. Pastry cream is another entry in the ephemeral-topping family alongside compote, icing, powdered sugar, whipped cream.
- [[chocolate-ganache]]: another rich made-in-advance topping — but ganache stores much better than pastry cream (weeks vs days), which is why ganache belongs on fridge-friendly cakes like [[greek-yogurt-lemon-pound-cake]] while pastry cream fits ephemeral-topping cakes.
